summary: A CBC Radio Quirks and Quarks segment (posted Dec 10, 2021) reports on a study by Adria LeBoeuf, an assistant professor of biology at the University of Fribourg, showing that ants regurgitate food to one another (trophallaxis). The exchange does more than feed the colony: it creates a 'social circulatory system' that carries nutrients, proteins, hormones and RNA, keeping colony members connected. An ant's role can be inferred from the proteins in its social stomach, with nurse ants showing higher levels of anti-aging proteins.
one_line: Ants share regurgitated food through trophallaxis, forming a 'social circulatory system' that links colony members, according to a Fribourg biologist's study.
key_facts: Feeding through regurgitation is called trophallaxis and is known in many animals, including many species of ant.
Ants have a foregut, midgut and hindgut; the midgut and hindgut handle digested food.
The foregut is known as the "social gut" because material is stored there before being vomited into another ant's mouth.
Adria LeBoeuf is an assistant professor of biology at the University of Fribourg in Switzerland.
LeBoeuf's study suggests trophallaxis creates a "social circulatory system" for the colony.
Beyond nutrients, ants pass along proteins, hormones, and fragments of genetic material called RNA through vomit.
In colonies the exchange of vomit can be seen happening 20 times in a minute.
The vomit is usually a clear liquid.
The role an individual ant plays in the colony can be determined by the contents of its social stomach, in particular the proteins it carries.
Nurse ants that care for the young generally were found to have higher amounts of anti-aging proteins than other ants.
LeBoeuf suggested the higher anti-aging protein levels may ensure that nurse ants survive to care for future generations.
The article was posted Dec 10, 2021 at 5:09 PM EST and was produced and written by Mark Crawley.
The accompanying photo shows carpenter ants, with one vomiting into the mouth of the other, submitted by Adria LeBoeuf.
